item.title: Ukraine says military Starlink disrupted again as US envoys meet Putin in Moscow
item.description:
Image source, Sputnik / Pool via AFPImage caption,
Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow is the latest of many trips the US envoys have made to see Vladimir PutinByLaura GozziPublished12 November 2026, 10:08 GMTUpdated 30 minutes ago
President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Ukraine's military is again facing "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv is struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.
It came as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a day after the latest talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
Zelensky told European leaders in Dublin that Ukraine was trying to clear up the Starlink situation with the American side.
But Zelensky added "some things" were already clear: "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going."
He did not elaborate further.
Starshield was developed and launched by Elon Musk's SpaceX company. It has come to play a vital role in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front-line.
A similar issue with connectivity affected the front line in late October and lasted about a week before it was fixed. It remained unclear who had ordered the temporary restrictions on Starlink services at the time, with US officials and SpaceX offering differing explanations.
Zelensky said the current disruption had been ongoing for several days and was "helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine".
Kushner and Witkoff are then expected to travel to Dublin to meet Zelensky.
Videos shared by Russian media on Thursday showed Kushner and Witkoff disembarking a plane and being welcomed by Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev with handshakes and hugs.
Later, they headed to the Kremlin where they met Putin and three of his senior advisors.

item.title: 'We've got to run': Inside ruined Ukraine power plant under constant drone threat
item.description:
'We've got to run': Inside ruined Ukraine power plant under constant drone threat

As peace talks between Ukraine and Russia continue, Ukrainians are facing a rolling schedule of planned power cuts because of intensified Russian attacks on their energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.
Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.
Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson visits one of the country's power stations on the front lines of the war. Devastated by a direct ballistic missile strike, repair work is hampered by frequent air raids.

item.title: Suspected bomb hoax threats force fresh evacuations of Italian schools
item.description:
Image source, EPAImage caption,
Bomb squads have searched many schools but no devices have been foundByPaulin KolaPublished3 hours ago
Schools across Italy have received bomb threats for the second day in a row, sparking fresh panic and evacuations.
Some 1,800 schools, from Milan in the north to Sicily in the south, reported receiving a similar threat to one that created chaos in Italy on Wednesday - even though no devices have been found anywhere.
The Italian government has advised schools that "in the absence of concrete evidence beyond the simple receipt of a mass email indicating a danger, buildings must not not be evacuated".
Schools in Scotland and Northern Ireland received threats on Wednesday, too. It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.
On Thursday morning, a bomb alert at a Calais rail station delayed international and national train services in northern France.
The latest incidents follow a series of bomb hoaxes last week against airports and airlines in a number of European countries.
Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
Wednesday's email threat - sent to 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 Italian state schools - was said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan".
Some officials say it originated in Taiwan.
A similar message sent to Italian schools on Thursday, again signed by Mikhail Andropov, is said to have been sent from the account of a teacher in the Philippines whose account is believed to have been hacked.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has spoken of "a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern".

item.title: Democrat Scott Colom makes history as Mississippi's first black senator since 19th Century
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Why Democrat Scott Colom’s Senate win in Mississippi is so significantByBrandon Drenon, Jackson, Mississippi and Sareen HabeshianPublished11 November 2026Updated 2 hours ago
Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.
Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be seated in the US Senate since Blanche Bruce served from 1875 to 1881.
Fewer than five thousand votes out of nearly a million counted separated him from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The result means the Democrats will hold 55 seats in the 100-member Senate, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.
Before Scott Colom, these two men were the last black US senators in Mississippi
Published1 hour ago
Colom, 43, won with 49.2% of the vote. Hyde-Smith, who received 48.7%, congratulated Colom in a video posted on X on Wednesday evening and wished him well.
"While this was not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters," she said.
The contest was not considered to be in play until the final weeks of the campaign, given President Donald Trump won the state in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.
Colom offered a victory speech on the campus of Tougaloo College, met by hundreds of cheering supporters standing side-by-side under the night sky.
Image source, Kyla Herrmannsen/BBCImage caption,
A crowd of supporters turned out to cheer Colom's win
Excitement filled the air as he thanked them for the support over the days of waiting for a result since the 4 November election.
"They did not believe a moment like this was possible, but I kept the faith," Colom said.

item.title: Millions of Ebola dollars missing with staff unpaid while virus spreads, charity says
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
MSF says that many frontline workers do not have the equipment they needByBasillioh RukangaPublished12 November 2026, 12:54 GMTUpdated 32 minutes ago
Hundreds of millions of dollars meant to help tackle Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo are not reaching the intended recipients, a medical charity has warned.
A report from Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said that while the outbreak remained "out of control", front-line workers were going unpaid, lacked proper training and were struggling with shortages of essential supplies.
It added that in some cases ambulances had run out of fuel.
More than 5,400 people have died and 11,000 infected with Ebola in DR Congo since the outbreak was declared in May.
This makes it the second-most deadly outbreak of the disease ever recorded.
MSF has urged the Congolese government and UN agencies to "strengthen oversight and accountability" to ensure money already disbursed is effectively utilised.
This means "ensuring response personnel are properly trained, paid, equipped, and supported, and directing resources towards areas where needs are greatest", it said.
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.
MSF's warning adds to concerns raised by Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) last month, when it said that $700m (£527m) out of $962m disbursed to organisations implementing Ebola response was unaccounted for.
At the time, Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya said it was too early to describe it as embezzlement, characterising the issue as a major transparency and financial reporting failure.
The Congolese health minister echoed these concerns, saying that aid agencies were required to provide details of their work so the ministry could provide oversight but that only 22% had done so.

item.title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Surgeon films damage in Nasser hospital in GazaByRushdi Abualouf, Gaza correspondent, Reporting fromIstanbul, David Gritten and Claire KeenanPublished12 November 2026, 03:32 GMTUpdated 1 hour ago
Six people have been killed and about 30 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.
The hospital's director said two missiles hit a building containing surgical wards and intensive care units overnight, but that one of the missiles did not explode.
The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".
The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.
Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".
Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.
Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.
Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.
Image caption,
Pictures showed extensive damage to an operating theatre, wards and a sleeping area for medics
The Nasser Medical Complex is located in the city of Khan Younis and is the largest hospital in southern Gaza, serving almost one million people.

item.title: Oranges investigated after four girls die in suspected Uganda school poisoning
item.description:
Image source, Uganda Police Force/XImage caption,
The school's head teacher has been arrested to assist with investigationsBySwaibu IbrahimBBC Africa, Reporting fromKampalaPublished8 hours ago
Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four pupils at a school in the capital Kampala which they suspect may be the result of poisoning.
The four girls, aged between nine and 11 years, died on Tuesday. Three of the pupils died at home while the fourth passed away while receiving emergency treatment at a hospital.
The head teacher at the school, Ta'aliim Primary School and Quran Memorisation Centre, has been arrested to assist with investigations.
According to the school, eight pupils had eaten oranges shared by a fellow pupil.
Five pupils, including the four who later died, started vomiting. The fifth is still in hospital.
Post-mortem examinations are being carried out to determine the exact cause of death.
A police spokesperson was quoted by local media as saying that detectives would visit the village where the oranges the pupils ate came from.
The centre has been cordoned off as a crime scene.
Ugandan media shared videos of grieving parents describing their children's final moments, with some accusing the school of failing to provide clear and timely information.
The police have offered condolences to the bereaved families and affected community and say more information will be provided in due course.
The tragedy comes at a time when concerns are mounting over health and safety conditions in schools across Uganda.
Previous cases involving suspected contaminated food and exposure to harmful substances have left pupils hospitalised with symptoms including stomach pain, vomiting and breathing difficulties.
The incidents have intensified calls for authorities to strengthen monitoring of school feeding schemes, improve hygiene standards and ensure safer learning environments for children.

item.title: British woman missing from cruise ship in Atlantic
item.description:
Image source, TUIImage caption,
The woman disappeared while on the Marella Voyager (file photo)ByTom McArthurPublished12 November 2026, 09:54 GMTUpdated 5 hours ago
A British woman has gone missing from a cruise ship while it was crossing the Atlantic, travel operator Tui has said.
The 72-year-old was last seen aboard Tui's Marella Voyager on Monday while the vessel was en route to the Caribbean. The ship could have travelled hundreds of miles in the time between when she was last seen to when she was reported missing.
Staff realised the passenger was missing on Tuesday, when they noticed her bed had not been slept in. The alarm was raised and a search carried out, Tui said in a statement.
It is understood the missing guest was then reported to the US Coast Guard, which asked the ship to continue to its crossing rather than reverse course and search for the woman.
Holidaymakers were told to abandon dinners, drinks and entertainment as the crew carried out an emergency headcount on Tuesday evening, the Daily Mail reports.
Passengers stood in lines of four while staff scanned boarding cards to verify the identity of every person on the ship, according to the newspaper.
The USCG Rescue Co-ordination Centre in Norfolk, Virginia has issued an alert calling on any ships nearby to "keep a sharp look out" for the woman, the Mail reports. The BBC has contacted the USCG for comment.
The Marella Voyager, carrying around 2,000 passengers and 800 crew, left Malaga on 4 November and is due to arrive in Antigua on Friday before calling at Dominica and finishing its voyage in Barbados on Sunday.
A spokeswoman for Marella Cruises said it was "deeply saddened" by the disappearance, adding: "Our thoughts are with the guest's loved ones at this very difficult time.
"We're supporting the authorities with their enquiries, and out of respect for the guest and their family, we won't be commenting further at this stage."

item.title: Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: Protesters and police clash in BarcelonaByNick Beake, Europe correspondent, Reporting fromMadrid, Guy Hedgecoe, Reporting fromMadrid and Alba MorgadePublished11 November 2026
Clashes have broken out between groups of masked men and police in Barcelona after tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike for 14 years, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living.
Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in the capital Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where footage showed masked men setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows as police fired tear gas.
Transport and other public services across Spain faced serious disruption.
Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.
The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."
There was a heavy police presence in the centre of Barcelona on Wednesday evening, with officers wearing helmets and riot shields.
Some of the disturbances took place in the Passeig de Gràcia, close to the iconic Plaça de Catalunya in the centre of the city.
Small fires burned in the middle of the streets as bins were set alight. Local media reported that a group of people fired fireworks towards police and looted shops including the Lego store. Protesters were also seen trying to enter the Apple Store.
The BBC spoke to a woman who attended the protests in Barcelona who said it was mostly very peaceful and "joyful". She said she was there to protest about the housing costs and that "there were a lot of children and old people there."

item.title: Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Moment teen rescued after six days in Australian bushBySimon Atkinson and Tiffanie Turnbull, Reporting fromSydneyPublished12 November 2026, 02:40 GMT
A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.
William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.
Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.
He was located on Thursday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".
Image source, Victoria Police
Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.
The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.
"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.
"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."
Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again."
Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive.
"It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.
